L6@P0: Recent technological advances in single-cell sequencing have
L7@P0: enabled the probing of regulatory maps through multiple
L8@P0: omics layers, such as chromatin accessibility (single-cell
L9@P0: ATAC-sequencing (scATAC-seq)1,2
L10@P0: ), DNA methylation (snmC-seq3,
L11@P0: sci-MET4
L12@P0: ) and the transcriptome (scRNA-seq5,6), offering a unique
L13@P0: opportunity to unveil the underlying regulatory bases for the functionalities of diverse cell types7
L14@P0: . While simultaneous assays have
L15@P0: recently emerged8–11, different omics are usually measured independently and produce unpaired data, which calls for effective and
L16@P0: efficient in silico multi-omics integration12,13.
L17@P0: Computationally, one major obstacle faced when integrating
L18@P0: unpaired multi-omics data (also known as diagonal integration)
L19@P0: is the distinct feature spaces of different modalities (for example, accessible chromatin regions in scATAC-seq versus genes in
L20@P0: scRNA-seq)14. A quick fix is to convert multimodality data into
L21@P0: one common feature space based on prior knowledge and apply
L22@P0: single-omics data integration methods15–18. Such explicit ‘feature
L23@P0: conversion’ is straightforward, but has been reported to result in
L24@P0: information loss19. Algorithms based on coupled matrix factorization circumvent explicit conversion but hardly handle more than
L25@P0: two omics layers20,21. An alternative option is to match cells from
L26@P0: different omics layers via nonlinear manifold alignment, which
L27@P0: removes the requirement of prior knowledge completely and could
L28@P0: reduce inter-modality information loss in theory22–25; however, this
L29@P0: technique has mostly been applied to relatively small datasets with
L30@P0: limited number of cell types.
L31@P0: The ever-increasing volume of data is another serious challenge26. Recently developed technologies can routinely generate
L32@P0: datasets at the scale of millions of cells27–29, whereas current integration methods have only been applied to datasets with much smaller
L33@P0: volumes15,17,20–23. To catch up with the growth in data throughput, computational integration methods should be designed with
L34@P0: scalability in mind.
L35@P0: Hereby, we introduce GLUE (graph-linked unified embedding),
L36@P0: a modular framework for integrating unpaired single-cell multiomics data and inferring regulatory interactions simultaneously.
L37@P0: By modeling the regulatory interactions across omics layers explicitly, GLUE bridges the gaps between various omics-specific feature
L38@P0: spaces in a biologically intuitive manner. Systematic benchmarks and
L39@P0: case studies demonstrate that GLUE is accurate, robust and scalable
L40@P0: for heterogeneous single-cell multi-omics data. Furthermore, GLUE
L41@P0: is designed as a generalizable framework that allows for easy extension and quick adoption to particular scenarios in a modular manner.
L42@P0: GLUE is publicly accessible at https://github.com/gao-lab/GLUE.
L43@P0: Results
L44@P0: Unpaired multi-omics integration via graph-guided embeddings. Inspired by previous studies, we model cell states as
L45@P0: low-dimensional cell embeddings learned through variational autoencoders30,31. Given their intrinsic differences in biological nature
L46@P0: and assay technology, each omics layer is equipped with a separate
L47@P0: autoencoder that uses a probabilistic generative model tailored to
L48@P0: the layer-specific feature space (Fig. 1 and Methods).
L49@P0: Taking advantage of prior biological knowledge, we propose the
L50@P0: use of a knowledge-based graph (‘guidance graph’) that explicitly
L51@P0: models cross-layer regulatory interactions for linking layer-specific
L52@P0: feature spaces; the vertices in the graph correspond to the features of
L53@P0: different omics layers, and edges represent signed regulatory interactions. For example, when integrating scRNA-seq and scATAC-seq
L54@P0: data, the vertices are genes and accessible chromatin regions (that
L55@P0: is, ATAC peaks), and a positive edge can be connected between an
L56@P0: accessible region and its putative downstream gene. Then, adversarial multimodal alignment of the cells is performed as an iterative
L57@P0: optimization procedure, guided by feature embeddings encoded
L58@P0: from the graph32 (Fig. 1 and Methods). Notably, when the iterative
L59@P0: process converges, the graph can be refined with inputs from the
L60@P0: alignment procedure and used for data-oriented regulatory inference (see below for more details).
L61@P0: Systematic benchmarking demonstrates superior performance. We first benchmarked GLUE against multiple popular
L62@P0: unpaired multi-omics integration methods15–18,23–25,33 using three
L63@P0: Multi-omics single-cell data integration and

L66@P0: Despite the emergence of experimental methods for simultaneous measurement of multiple omics modalities in single cells,
L67@P0: most single-cell datasets include only one modality. A major obstacle in integrating omics data from multiple modalities is
L68@P0: that different omics layers typically have distinct feature spaces. Here, we propose a computational framework called GLUE
L69@P0: (graph-linked unified embedding), which bridges the gap by modeling regulatory interactions across omics layers explicitly.
L70@P0: Systematic benchmarking demonstrated that GLUE is more accurate, robust and scalable than state-of-the-art tools for heterogeneous single-cell multi-omics data. We applied GLUE to various challenging tasks, including triple-omics integration, integrative regulatory inference and multi-omics human cell atlas construction over millions of cells, where GLUE was able to correct
L71@P0: previous annotations. GLUE features a modular design that can be flexibly extended and enhanced for new analysis tasks. The
L72@P0: full package is available online at https://github.com/gao-lab/GLUE.

L203@P2: In addition to the systematical difference among omics layers, single-cell data are often complicated by batch effect within
L204@P2: the same layer. For example, the SHARE-seq data was processed
L205@P2: in four libraries, one of which showed batch effect compared to
L206@P2: the other three in scRNA-seq (Supplementary Fig. 6a), while the
L207@P2: Nephron data profiled four donors, all of which showed substantial
L208@P2: batch effect against each other in both scRNA-seq and scATAC-seq
L209@P2: (Supplementary Fig. 7a,c). As a solution to such complex scenarios, GLUE provides batch correction capability by including
L210@P2: batch as a decoder covariate (Methods). With batch correction
L211@P2: enabled, GLUE was able to correct for these batch effects effectively, producing substantially better batch mixing (Supplementary
L212@P2: Fig. 6b and Supplementary Fig. 7b,d). To guard against potential
L213@P2: over-correction, for example, when forcing an integration over
L214@P2: datasets lacking common cell states, we devised a diagnostic metric
L215@P2: called the integration consistency score, which measures the consistency between the integrated multi-omics space and prior knowledge in the guidance graph (Methods). We observed substantially
L216@P2: lower scores (close to 0) when integrating data from inconsistent
L217@P2: tissues compared to integrating within the same tissue, making it a
L218@P2: reliable indicator of integration quality (Extended Data Fig. 6).
L219@P2: GLUE enables effective triple-omics integration. Benefitting from

L222@P2: adult mouse cortex, including gene expression37, chromatin accessibility38 and DNA methylation3

L347@P3: of cell states across the three omics layers (Fig. 3a–d). Notably, the
L348@P3: original cell types were not annotated at the same resolution, and

L353@P3: marker overlap (Fig. 3e, three-way Fisher’s exact test40, false discovery rate (FDR)<5×10−17) for 12 out of the 14 mapped cell types
